description: Test your knowledge of MI11.1-3 | Antimicrobial Resistance & Stewardship.

cards.text: What is intrinsic resistance and how does it differ from acquired resistance?
cards.answer: Intrinsic resistance is a natural, inherent property present before antibiotic exposure; acquired resistance develops through mutation or horizontal gene transfer during treatment.

tip.tip: Intrinsic = built-in from species origin; Acquired = developed or borrowed

cards.text: Why are Gram-negative bacteria intrinsically resistant to penicillin G?
cards.answer: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria excludes the hydrophobic penicillin G molecule, preventing it from reaching its cell wall target.

tip.tip: Outer membrane = protective barrier; Penicillin G = too lipophilic to penetrate

cards.text: Which mechanism of horizontal gene transfer is most clinically critical and why?
cards.answer: Conjugation (plasmid transfer via sex pilus) is most clinically critical because it spreads resistance genes across unrelated species in ICUs (e.g., NDM-1, MCR colistin resistance).

tip.tip: Conjugation = direct cell contact; fastest spread between different bacteria

cards.text: Explain the principle of the Kirby-Bauer (disk diffusion) method.
cards.answer: Antibiotic-impregnated disks are placed on Mueller-Hinton agar; antibiotic diffuses outward creating a zone of inhibition. Zone diameter is measured and compared to CLSI breakpoints to determine susceptibility.

tip.tip: Bigger zone = more antibiotic diffusion = more susceptible organism

cards.text: What do the three AST result categories (S, I, R) mean for clinical practice?
cards.answer: S (Susceptible) = standard dosing will achieve therapeutic levels; I (Intermediate) = higher dose needed; R (Resistant) = standard therapy will fail, alternate antibiotic required.

tip.tip: S = use normally; I = use cautiously/higher dose; R = avoid

cards.text: Define MIC and identify the gold standard method for measuring it.
cards.answer: MIC (Minimum Inhibitory Concentration) is the lowest antibiotic concentration preventing visible bacterial growth. Broth microdilution (BMD) is the gold standard method for precise measurement.

tip.tip: MIC = lowest drug dose that stops growth; BMD = most accurate method

cards.text: Give an example of mutation-based resistance in tuberculosis.
cards.answer: rpoB gene mutations in M. tuberculosis alter the drug binding site, causing rifampicin resistance detectable by GeneXpert. This resistance is clonal and cannot transfer to other species.

tip.tip: rpoB mutation = rifampicin-resistant TB; clonal = not contagious to other bacteria

cards.text: Why is an organism's MIC value important for antibiotic dosing decisions?
cards.answer: MIC enables pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) target attainment assessment — determining if standard doses achieve sufficient free drug concentration at the infection site (e.g., >4× MIC for meropenem).

tip.tip: MIC guides dosing: match achievable drug level to organism's resistance level
